messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Horizontal distance (range) after a time \(t\)**  

If a car (or any projectile) is launched from the ground with an initial speed \(v\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, its horizontal component of velocity is

\[
v_x = v\cos\theta .
\]

Because horizontal velocity is constant (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal distance travelled after a time \(t\) is simply

\[
\boxed{\,x(t)=v\cos\theta \; t\, } .
\]

---

### Vertical motion (for reference)

The vertical component of velocity is

\[
v_y(t)=v\sin\theta - g\,t ,
\]

so the vertical displacement after time \(t\) is

\[
y(t)=v\sin\theta \; t-\frac12 g t^{2}.
\]

---

### Total distance along the trajectory (arc length)

If you really want the *arc length* of the path up to time \(t\), you would integrate the speed:

\[
s(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\sqrt{(v\cos\theta)^2+\bigl(v\sin\theta-g\tau\bigr)^2}\;d\tau .
\]

This integral has a closed‑form expression involving logarithms and square roots, but it is rarely needed unless you’re doing a detailed physics simulation.

---

### Quick sanity check

| \(v\) (m/s) | \(\theta\) (°) | \(t\) (s) | \(x(t)\) (m) |
|-------------|----------------|-----------|--------------|
| 20          | 30             | 2         | \(20\cos30^\circ \times 2 \approx 34.6\) |
| 50          | 45             | 1.5       | \(50\cos45^\circ \times 1.5 \approx 53.0\) |

---

#### What if you want the *full* range (until landing)?

The time of flight is

\[
t_{\text{flight}}=\frac{2v\sin\theta}{g},
\]

and the horizontal range is

\[
R=\frac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}.
\]

But since you asked for a specific time \(t\), the simple formula \(x(t)=v\cos\theta\,t\) is what you need.
